title: The Mondragon Cooperatives
text:
In 1941 a young Catholic priest, Jose Maria Arizmendiarrieta, was sent to Mondragon, a town in the Basque Country of Spain still poor and divided after the Civil War. He decided that the best way to help was education and work. In 1943 he founded a small technical school for local boys.

In 1956 five of its graduates, with his support, started a company to make paraffin heaters and stoves. It was organized as a worker cooperative: the workers themselves owned it, each invested capital, and each had one vote in the general assembly, regardless of position. Pay differences between the highest and lowest paid were kept small. The firm, later called Fagor, prospered.

Arizmendiarrieta saw that cooperatives needed their own institutions to survive. In 1959 the group founded a cooperative bank, the Caja Laboral Popular, which drew savings from the region and lent them to new cooperatives, along with technical advice. A cooperative social security system followed. When one cooperative lost business, members could be moved to others rather than simply laid off.

Over the following decades the network grew into one of Spain's largest business groups, with manufacturing, retail, finance and a university, owned by tens of thousands of worker-members. It has had failures too: in 2013 its flagship appliance maker, Fagor Electrodomesticos, went bankrupt. But the group survived, and its members were largely relocated within it.
lesson: People who own and govern their workplace together can build a lasting enterprise. Shared ownership works best with shared institutions that support each other in hard times.
people: Jose Maria Arizmendiarrieta, founders of Ulgor (Fagor)
source: William Foote Whyte and Kathleen King Whyte, Making Mondragon (1988)
